question_of_class.title: The question of class
questions: Thompson turned against an economistic Marxism in which class follows from the base. What did he put in its place when he called class "a relationship, and not a thing", and what evidence does that require?
Is class a structure, a relationship, an experience or a language? Which entries on this pathway answer differently?

In the 1987 International Labor and Working-Class History forum, Joan Scott argued for reading class through language and gender, and Bryan Palmer answered her. What exactly did they disagree about, and what would each accept as evidence?

Joy Parr's Gender of Breadwinners (1990) studies a knitting town where women were the breadwinners and a furniture town where men were. Does treating gender and class together, in particular places, settle the Scott–Palmer quarrel or sidestep it?
What does the linguistic turn's account of the 'languages of class' keep from Thompson, and what does Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) say it gives up?
Chakrabarty argues that Bengal jute workers do not fit a universal story of class formation. Is that a critique of Marxist categories or a demand to use them differently?

Does Canadian working-class history need its own frame? Palmer criticises McKay's liberal order for letting historians avoid capitalism; is liberal order a way of putting class back at the centre or of moving it aside?
question_of_class.exercise: Take one primary source about work or labour protest. Read it first as evidence of class formation (Thompson), then through language and gender (Scott), then as Palmer would answer Scott, and finally as Parr would place it in a particular town's gendered labour market. Which conclusions survive all four readings?
